extracted.intended_audience: readers of an early-18th-century periodical / coffee-house literate public (readers of The Tatler/Spectator-style essays)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, discursive periodical essays and social criticism written for the coffee-house/periodical readership, combining news, moral commentary, and literary criticism. Targets style, topicality, and civic usefulness in short essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panegyric: artful indirect praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of panegyric consists in a certain artful way of conveying the applause in an indirect manner; taking a man by surprise, and being welcome when you have so surprised him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: praise should be conveyed indirectly so the subject is taken unawares, producing a sudden favourable change in sentiment (example: the senator proposing Tiberius be declared a god). Effect: the person flattered receives you into favour at once. Anti-pattern: obvious, direct flattery (the company mocked the pamphlet 'The Naked Truth' for appearing to promise plain dealing but actually praising the great).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit must be allied to virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: When Virgil describes a wit, he always means a virtuous man; the wisest man was the greatest wit; none was thought worthy of that character unless he answered the poet's description (one who subdues fear and fate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for 'wit': not mere cleverness but moral greatness — contempt of low fears and mean gratifications. Application: a true man of genius places happiness in moral superiority rather than sensual or trivial pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure requires severity/moderation (decency)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain severity in pleasure (res est severa voluptas). Without that, all decency is banished; if reason is not present at our greatest satisfactions, the human is the most miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative rule for social behaviour and entertainments: pleasures should be moderated by reason and decorum. Anti-pattern: indulgent, unregulated pleasure that abandons decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage morality and genre-appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is against all morality, as well as rules of the stage, that Punch should be in jest in the Deluge, or indeed that he should appear at all (i.e., comic buffoonery is improper in a tragic or solemn representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for theatrical/puppet performances: maintain moral appropriateness and respect genre boundaries. Example: audience hissed at the puppet-show for mixing Punch's comedy into Noah's flood; critics may call out breaches of 'rules of the stage.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in public inscriptions and signage
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross errors in the very directions of things are intolerable; inscriptions on sign-posts are often misspelt or ill-painted, misleading strangers (example: 'This is the BEER' vs 'This is the BEAR').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard: public-facing text and imagery should be correctly spelled and painted; mistakes cause real-world misdirection and inconvenience. Remedy suggested: apply learning to correct such obvious errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholars should apply learning to useful public tasks (public spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of wit spend too much on fine speculations while neglecting obvious things useful to mankind; it would be happy if those with capacities were employed in works of general use—because 'everybody's business is nobody's business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm for intellectuals/men of letters: prioritize practical, public-benefit tasks (e.g., correcting public signs) over vain pedantry. Anti-pattern: endless quibbling over minute scholarly points while public needs go unattended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest self-denial by inventors may be a social virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A benefactor who shuns glory—by making his name obscene to avoid being spoken—has gained reputation by self-denial; some inventors avoid applause purposely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative note about character and reputation: refusal of public applause (modesty/self-denial) can itself be a mark of esteem among 'modern wits.' Example: a surgeon who invented an engine and made it 'an immodesty to name his name' is ranked highly by contemporaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must fit content and audience (don't obscure intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A title or claim (e.g., 'Naked Truth') should match the actual manner of discourse; a work promising plain dealing but written in sublime, obscure language fails its implied promise and may not reach the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for pamphlets and prose: ensure honesty between promise and execution; technical/highly elevated rhetoric that conceals panegyric or is unintelligible to the 'vulgar' is a flaw. Example: critics mocked 'Naked Truth' for elevated style that disguised praise; anti-pattern: obscurity used to hide true purpose.
